Google Trends uses a sample of searches; data is anonymized, aggregated, and normalized to 0–100. Same score across regions does not mean same number of searches.
A region indicates relative interest attributed to that geography. It does NOT expose an IP address, person, agency, government, or organization.
Niche terms may have too little volume for stable graphs. Treat one-off obscure-name spikes as hypotheses until independently reproduced/exported.
Literal search-term runs must be distinguished from Topics. Full names, short names, and compound queries must be tested separately.
Common names need qualifiers and matched controls.
A pre-event search is less surprising if the relevant role was already publicly announced.
Compare case subjects with case-related people who show no anomaly and with similarly obscure unrelated names matched by public profile.
Compare anomaly frequency per person-query-day across case subjects vs controls; stratify by name rarity, public profile, geography, query type, and date-window length.
For future results save exact Explore URL/settings, download CSV, capture screenshot, timestamp, geography level, search type, category, and date range.
Do not infer foreknowledge, conspiracy, government involvement, or a specific searcher from a Trends spike alone.
